# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Definition and Epidemiology

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) was first systematically defined in 2000, when a National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) and Office of Rare Diseases workshop proposed four diagnostic criteria: heart failure (HF) in the last month of pregnancy or within five months of delivery, absence of another identifiable cause, absence of recognizable heart disease before the last month of pregnancy, and echocardiographic left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction.Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a rare life-threatening cardiomyopathy of unknown cause that occurs in the peripartum period in previously healthy women, and in April 1997 the NHLBI and the Office of Rare Diseases of the NIH convened a Workshop on Peripartum Cardiomyopathy to develop recommendations for research and education. In 2010, the Heart Failure Association (HFA) of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Working Group broadened this definition. The 2010 Heart Failure Association of the European Society of Cardiology Working Group revised the definition of PPCM to "an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with HF secondary to LV systolic dysfunction towards the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, where no other cause of heart failure is found." The diagnostic criteria indicate that LVEF is <45% and there may or may not be ventricular dilatation. A modified echocardiographic definition has also been applied in clinical practice.Hibbard, Lindheimer and Lang proposed a modified definition for peripartum cardiomyopathy and prognosis based on echocardiography.

PPCM remains fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion. PPCM is a diagnosis of exclusion in women presenting with HF due to LV systolic dysfunction and should be considered when no other cause is evident. Its incidence varies markedly with geography and ethnicity. PPCM occurs in approximately 1:3,000 live births in the United States although some series report a much higher incidence, and African-American women are particularly at risk. Early and late presentations appear clinically similar.Elkayam et al. described pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy: clinical characteristics and a comparison between early and late presentation (Circulation 2005;111:2050-2055). An authoritative seminar summarized the global clinical picture.Sliwa, Fett and Elkayam published a Lancet seminar on peripartum cardiomyopathy in 2006.

## Pathophysiology

The leading mechanistic paradigm is the "vasculo-hormonal" hypothesis. In mice with cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of stat3, cardiac cathepsin D expression and activity is enhanced and associated with the generation of a cleaved antiangiogenic and proapoptotic 16 kDa form of prolactin; treatment with bromocriptine prevents the development of PPCM, whereas forced myocardial generation of 16 kDa prolactin impairs the cardiac capillary network and function. This fragment exerts downstream effects through microRNA signaling.Halkein et al. demonstrated that microRNA-146a is a therapeutic target and biomarker for peripartum cardiomyopathy (J Clin Invest 2013;123:2143-2154).

A complementary angiogenic-imbalance model implicates placental antiangiogenic factors. PPCM is associated with a systemic angiogenic imbalance accentuated by pre-eclampsia; mice lacking cardiac PGC-1α develop profound PPCM, and the cardiomyopathy is entirely rescued by pro-angiogenic therapies. In humans, the placenta in late gestation secretes VEGF inhibitors like soluble FLT1 (sFLT1), accentuated by multiple gestation and pre-eclampsia; this anti-angiogenic environment is accompanied by subclinical cardiac dysfunction correlating with circulating sFLT1, and exogenous sFLT1 alone caused profound systolic dysfunction in mice lacking cardiac PGC-1α. Vascular mediators also track with clinical course in patients: higher relaxin-2 levels soon after delivery were associated with myocardial recovery at 2 months, whereas higher sFlt1 levels correlated with more severe symptoms and major adverse clinical events. A comprehensive review of pathophysiology and epidemiology integrates these strands.PPCM is a potentially life-threatening heart disease that emerges towards the end of pregnancy or in the first months postpartum in previously healthy women, with symptoms and signs similar to idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy.

A genetic predisposition is now firmly established. In 172 women with PPCM, sequencing of 43 dilated-cardiomyopathy genes found a prevalence of truncating variants (26 in 172 [15%]) significantly higher than in a reference population (4.7%) but similar to a dilated cardiomyopathy cohort (17%). TTN truncating variants were the most prevalent genetic predisposition in each disorder, and their presence correlated with a lower ejection fraction at 1-year follow-up.

## Diagnosis and Risk Factors

Because the symptoms of normal late pregnancy overlap with HF, diagnosis is frequently delayed. Delays in diagnosis may occur because the symptoms and signs of PPCM can mimic the normal findings of late pregnancy and the peripartum period. As shortness of breath, fatigue and leg oedema are common in the peripartum period, a high index of suspicion is required not to miss the diagnosis; measurement of natriuretic peptides, electrocardiography and echocardiography are recommended to promptly diagnose or exclude HF/PPCM. Recognized risk factors include pre-eclampsia and multiple gestation, consistent with the sFLT1 mechanism.sFlt1 levels are markedly elevated in women with preeclampsia, likely in part explaining why preeclampsia is such a strong risk factor for PPCM. Key differential diagnoses must be excluded.Important differential diagnoses include pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, hypertensive heart disease during pregnancy, and pre-existing heart disease.

## Management

Acute and chronic care follows guideline-directed HF therapy, modified for pregnancy and lactation, ideally within a multidisciplinary framework, as detailed in the 2019 HFA position statement.PPCM is a potentially life-threatening condition typically presenting as HF with reduced ejection fraction in the last month of pregnancy or the months following delivery in women without another known cause; this updated position statement summarizes pathophysiological mechanisms, risk factors, clinical presentation, diagnosis and management. Disease-specific therapy with bromocriptine targets the prolactin pathway. A prospective, single-center, randomized, open-label, proof-of-concept pilot study compared standard care (n=10) versus standard care plus bromocriptine for 8 weeks (n=10). At 6 months, recovery of LV ejection fraction was greater in the bromocriptine group (from 27% to 58% vs. from 27% to 36%, P = 0.012). A subsequent multicentre randomized study compared two regimens. Bromocriptine treatment was associated with a high rate of full LV recovery and low morbidity and mortality compared with other PPCM cohorts; no significant differences were observed between 1-week and 8-week treatment, suggesting that 1-week addition of bromocriptine to standard HF treatment is already beneficial with a trend favoring full recovery in the 8-week group. More recently, registry data have re-examined efficacy. While bromocriptine presents a promising pathophysiology-based disease-specific treatment option, the evidence regarding its efficacy remains limited; the EORP PPCM registry analysis aimed to determine whether bromocriptine treatment is associated with improved maternal outcomes.

## Outcomes and Counseling

Prognosis is heterogeneous but generally favorable with modern care. In the IPAC study, 100 women with PPCM were followed through 1 year postpartum; event-free survival at 1 year was 93%, transplant-free survival was 95%, and at 12 months 72% achieved an LVEF ≥50%. Global registries confirm broadly similar presentations worldwide. The first international registry showed that patient presentations were similar globally, with heterogeneity in patient management and outcome. The ESC EORP registry reported clinical presentation, management, and 6-month outcomes across diverse populations.This ESC EORP registry sought to describe the clinical presentation, management, and 6-month outcomes in women with PPCM globally. Subsequent pregnancies carry substantial risk, particularly when LV function has not normalized.Elkayam et al. reported maternal and fetal outcomes of subsequent pregnancies in women with peripartum cardiomyopathy (N Engl J Med 2001;344:1567-1571). Recovery within months is common.Despite a mortality rate of up to 10% and a high risk of relapse in subsequent pregnancies, many patients with PPCM recover within 3 to 6 months of disease onset.

## Conclusion

PPCM is a potentially fatal but frequently recoverable form of pregnancy-associated HF. Despite extensive research, diagnosing and managing PPCM remains challenging; recent advances include molecular biomarkers, genetic risk prediction, targeted therapies, multidisciplinary care, and improved patient education. Convergent evidence supports a "two-hit" model combining peripartum antiangiogenic signaling with host genetic susceptibility, and ongoing trials will further clarify the role of disease-specific therapy.
